Our visual system does not report the light that reaches the eye. It estimates the color of the surface, and because it knows that B lies in the shadow of the cylinder, it corrects for the shadow. A camera makes no such correction. It records the light.

The illusion holds two lessons for color features. First, the numbers in an image file are measurements of light, not of perception, so we must transform them before their distances become meaningful. Second, a feature must decide which differences to ignore: a shadow changes the measured color of a surface, but not the surface itself. This section explains how three numbers come to describe a color, shows why the space in which we compare them decides whether distances make sense, and then builds the two classic color features, histograms and moments. Research has proposed many more, such as color correlograms and dominant-color descriptors, but most of them lost their relevance once learned features took over (
). Histograms and moments are enough to show the ideas that all color features share.

The light that reaches the eye from a point in the scene is the product of the illumination and the reflectance of the surface. Snow reflects almost all visible wavelengths, vegetation reflects mostly green, and water reflects little. The result is a spectrum: an energy value for every wavelength between about 380 and 780 nanometers. The eye does not measure this spectrum. The retina has three types of cones, and each type responds to a broad band of wavelengths (

). The S (short-wavelength) cones peak near 420 nm, the M (medium) cones near 534 nm, and the L (long) cones near 564 nm. They are often called the blue, green, and red cones, although the L cones peak in the yellow-green; they respond more strongly to red light than the other two types. Each cone type weights the spectrum with its sensitivity curve and sums the result, so the whole spectrum is reduced to three numbers.

children.alt: The eye, the photoreceptors of the retina, and the spectral sensitivity of the three cone types and the rods.

children.value: The eye, the photoreceptors of the retina, and the spectral sensitivity of the three cone types and the rods.
Reducing a spectrum to three numbers loses information. Two different spectra can produce the same three cone responses, and then they look identical. This effect is called

, and every display relies on it: a monitor mixes red, green, and blue light so that the cones respond as they would to the original scene, although the two spectra have little in common. Metamerism is also the reason why three channels per pixel are enough for an image file. A color is a point in a three-dimensional space, and color features describe how the pixels of an image are distributed in that space. The appendix covers the human visual system in
and the definitions of all color spaces in
The obvious choice is the space the file already uses: sRGB, with three values from 0 to 255 per pixel.

shows four colors where one channel changes by 100 units from one box to the next. In sRGB, all three steps have the same Euclidean distance of 100. To the eye, they are not equal. The step from the olive green (155, 200, 100) to the golden yellow (255, 200, 100) looks large, while the step from the salmon (255, 100, 100) to the crimson (255, 0, 100) looks much smaller. The sRGB scale was defined to match the response of monitors, not perception, so equal distances do not mean equal differences.

The conversions from sRGB to Lab or HSV are fixed formulas that every image library provides. The conversion to Lab has one step that is easy to miss: sRGB values are gamma-encoded and must be linearized before they are converted to CIE XYZ and then to Lab.

The division makes the histogram independent of the image size, so a thumbnail and the full-resolution photo have nearly the same histogram. Because the histogram ignores where a pixel lies, shifting, rotating, or mirroring the image does not change it either.

The Matterhorn photo uses 40 of the 125 reference colors, and three of them cover almost two thirds of its pixels. The light sky blue (37.6%) covers the sky and the snow in shade, white (14.0%) the sunlit snow and the clouds, and a dark blue-gray (12.0%) the forest slopes in shadow. The Taj Mahal photo contains the same kinds of colors: blue sky, light marble, and dark shadows. They fall into different bins, though. Its sky is darker than the Matterhorn’s: it lands in the two blue bins one and two lightness ranges lower (19.4% and 10.0%), and at the position of the Matterhorn’s largest bin, the Taj Mahal histogram is almost empty (0.01%). The Federer photo is dominated by a single yellowish green, the grass, with 57.2% of the pixels.

The three measures applied to the 125-bin histograms of the Matterhorn, Taj Mahal, and Federer photos give the following values:

All three measures rank the Taj Mahal closer to the Matterhorn than the Federer photo, but they differ in how clearly. The bin-by-bin measures see two very different histograms in both cases: only 32% of the Taj Mahal histogram overlaps with the Matterhorn histogram. The reason is the bin boundary visible in

: the slightly darker sky of the Taj Mahal photo falls into the lightness ranges below the Matterhorn’s sky. The palette query shows the same effect: it scores the Taj Mahal photo only 0.06, although its sky is clearly blue. The quadratic distance accounts for the similarity of neighboring bins and puts the Taj Mahal more than four times closer than the Federer photo.

The result is a success and a failure at the same time. The histogram works as designed, and it returns a building when the query shows a mountain. Perceptual similarity is not semantic similarity: a feature that measures how an image looks finds images that look alike, which is not the same as images that show the same thing.
A histogram with 125 bins is a long vector, and practical systems use up to a thousand bins.

The moments have very different value ranges: standard deviations of 5 to 30, skewness values around 1, covariances of up to about 140. Before a Euclidean or Manhattan distance can compare two moment vectors, each dimension must be rescaled, for example with the Gaussian normalization of

, which divides each dimension by its standard deviation over the collection. Two variants reduce the vector further. Moments of the lightness alone give 4 values and ignore color. Moments of the two chromaticity channels

Compared with histograms, moments are compact: 15 values instead of 125 to 1000 bins, and no cross-bin matrix is needed. They share the robustness of histograms against shifts, rotations, and scaling. Their weakness is that a few statistics cannot describe a distribution with several peaks. The bright sky and the dark forest of the Matterhorn photo average to a lightness of 60.9, a value that few of its pixels actually have. The appendix shows how all moments are computed in a single pass over the pixels (

Histograms and moments ignore where a color occurs. A blue lake at the bottom of a photo counts the same as a blue sky at the top, and shuffling the pixels of an image produces a meaningless image with exactly the same features. A simple remedy keeps a little layout information. Stricker and Dimai proposed in 1996 to split the image into five overlapping regions, an ellipse in the center and the four corners, to compute color moments per region, and to weight the center more strongly. Such features remain cheap and work well for photos with a typical composition, where the subject sits in the middle.

The deeper limitation is that color says nothing about structure. The pyramid shape of the Matterhorn, the sharp ridges, the grain of the forest: all of this lies in how the intensities are arranged, not in which colors occur. The next section turns to features that describe this arrangement.
